opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it's interesting, because at the beginning I don't think we framed it as "data scientists are our market." It came out of what we were doing at Berkeley with Spark. Spark started in the AMPLab, and the early users were people who had a lot of data and wanted to do something more sophisticated than just SQL queries: machine learning, iterative algorithms, interactive exploration. Hadoop MapReduce was really painful for that, because every iteration you went back to disk. So the people who felt that pain most acutely were the people doing what we'd now call data science.

When we started Databricks, the natural question was: who gets the most value from this? Data engineers were obviously important, because someone has to build the pipelines. But the people who were really stuck, who had the questions but couldn't get answers fast enough, were the data scientists. They wanted to work in Python, in notebooks, iterate quickly, and not think about clusters, configuration, or tuning the JVM. So a big part of the early product was hiding the infrastructure: you open a notebook, you have a cluster, you write some code, and it just works on large data.

Looking back, there were pros and cons. On the plus side, data scientists were very enthusiastic. They'd adopt new tools quickly, and they were vocal, so you got good word of mouth. On the minus side, at the time it wasn't always a big budget line in many enterprises. A lot of companies had a few data scientists, and they were often doing exploratory work that wasn't yet in production. So the spend wasn't where the data warehouse spend or the ETL spend was.

Over time we realized you can't really separate these personas. To do good data science or machine learning, you need clean, reliable data, which means data engineering. And once you have that data, people also want to run SQL and BI on it. That's a big part of what led to the lakehouse idea: instead of having a data lake for the data scientists and a separate warehouse for the analysts, with data copied back and forth, you want one platform where all these personas work on the same data.

So data scientists were a great entry point. They were the people with the most acute pain and they loved the technology. But to build a big business, we had to expand to the data engineers and eventually the analysts. And now, with generative AI, it's coming full circle, because AI is again at the center, and everyone in the organization wants to build on top of their data.

r001.rationale: The response explains data scientists’ early pain, adoption, and product fit, but does not identify universities introducing data science degree programs as a signal of future market potential.

fable-5.1.text:
Ion Stoica: So to be honest, in the beginning we didn't think of it in terms of a market in a very structured way. We came out of the AMPLab at Berkeley, and we had built Spark, and the people who were using Spark were the ones who had this very painful problem, which is: you have a lot of data, it doesn't fit on one machine, and you want to do something more than just run SQL queries on it. You want to build models, you want to iterate, you want to explore. And the tools that existed for that at the time, mostly Hadoop and MapReduce, were really built for engineers. They were very low level. If you were a statistician or someone coming from the R or Python world, it was almost impossible.

So the data scientists sort of found us. They were the early adopters because they were in the most pain. And I think one of the reasons they were in such pain is that this was the period when everyone was starting to talk about big data, companies were collecting huge amounts of data, hiring these people, and then handing them a Hadoop cluster and saying, go find insights. And they couldn't be productive. They would write something, it would take hours to run, they'd find a bug, and start again.

Spark fixed that in a couple of ways. One was performance, the in-memory execution, so you could actually iterate. But I think the more important one, which we underestimated at first, was the API. You could write code that looked like normal programs, in Scala, in Python, later in R, and it just ran at scale. For a data scientist, that was the thing. They didn't want to learn a new paradigm, they wanted their existing way of working to not break when the data got big.

Now, when we started the company, there was a question of, okay, do we go after the people who already use Spark, these early adopters, or do we try to appeal to a broader audience. And our view was, you start with the people who love you. The data scientists who were using Spark were very vocal, they were going to meetups, they were writing blog posts, they were pushing their companies to adopt it. So from a go-to-market perspective, that was a huge advantage. We didn't have to convince them about the problem. They came to us.

The other thing I'd say is that we realized pretty early that the data scientists themselves were not really the buyers. They were the users, and they were the champions, but the budget usually sat with whoever owned the data infrastructure. So we had to think about both. We had to make a product that the data scientist loved, with notebooks, with collaboration, with being able to just get a cluster without asking IT. And at the same time we had to make it something that the infrastructure team and eventually the CIO would be comfortable with, in terms of security, in terms of cost, in terms of how it fit with the rest of their stack.

And honestly, that tension was one of the things that shaped the product for years. Because if you only serve the data scientist, you end up with something that's great for a demo and very hard to put in production. And if you only serve the infrastructure people, you end up with another platform that nobody wants to use. So the initial market was data scientists, yes, but the lesson was that you can't stop there. You have to use them as the wedge and then expand to data engineers and to the analysts, which is really what led us later to this whole idea of unifying all of it in one place.

r001.rationale: The response says companies were hiring data scientists and those users became early adopters, but it does not identify universities introducing data science degree programs as a signal of a promising future market.

astra-6.text:
We thought data scientists were a natural place to start because they needed to work with data at scale, but a lot of their effort went into getting the infrastructure to work. Before they could explore the data or build a model, they had to deal with setting up clusters and managing software. We wanted to make that much easier so they could focus on the actual analysis.

But a data scientist doesn’t work in isolation. They depend on people preparing the data, and then they need to collaborate with engineers to put their work into production. So the initial focus was on data scientists, but the broader opportunity was to bring those people together around the same data and the same platform.

r001.rationale: The response explains why data scientists were a natural initial market and describes their infrastructure needs, but it does not mention universities introducing data science degree programs as a market signal.

sol-6.1.text:
We saw data scientists as the people who were running into these problems first. They wanted to work with large amounts of data, explore it interactively, and build models, but they were spending a lot of their time setting up infrastructure and moving data between tools. Spark gave them a powerful engine, but you still had to install it, configure a cluster, and keep it running.

Our idea was to take that complexity away, so they could focus on the data and the algorithms. And the collaborative aspect was important: a data scientist rarely works alone. They need to work with data engineers and, eventually, get their work into production. So data scientists were the initial entry point, but the broader opportunity was to make that whole workflow much easier.

r001.rationale: The response describes data scientists’ practical problems and their role as Databricks’ initial market, but it does not mention universities introducing data science degree programs as a signal of future market potential.
